analysis.one_liner: Lets people sue federal officers who stop them from filming or watching police in public.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with a single cosponsor, has sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee since June 2026 with no vote and no committee action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write into law an explicit right to film, watch, or peacefully protest federal law enforcement in public, and would let people sue federal officers who interfere with that right. A person who wins could collect at least $25,000 even without proving actual harm, plus up to $100,000 in punitive damages for malicious violations, and the federal government itself could be held liable even when the officer would otherwise have legal immunity. It would also require annual training for federal officers on respecting the right to record.
analysis.who_benefits: Bystanders, protesters, and journalists who film or observe federal law enforcement — including immigration agents — would gain a clear way to sue when officers threaten, detain, seize their phones, or retaliate against them for recording. The bill makes the United States itself pay damages and covers attorney's fees, so a person would not need deep pockets to bring a case. Plaintiffs could collect $25,000 in statutory damages per violation without proving they suffered a specific loss, and could still pursue other claims under federal or state law.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Bystanders, protesters, and journalists filming police

how_it_helps.text: Creates an express federal cause of action when a federal officer prevents recording, threatens or surveils a person in retaliation, seizes a phone or footage, or arrests someone for filming, with a minimum of $25,000 in statutory damages per violation even without proof of actual harm.

Waives sovereign immunity so the United States itself is liable for an officer's conduct, even if the officer has an immunity defense, and separately keeps individual officers on the hook for damages including up to $100,000 in punitive damages for malicious violations.
Requires courts to award reasonable attorney's fees and costs to a prevailing plaintiff, so ordinary people can afford to bring these cases.

Requires the head of every federal law enforcement agency to train all officers annually, within one year of enactment, on enforcing the law while respecting the right to record, observe, or peacefully protest.
States the sense of Congress that the First Amendment already protects recording law enforcement, and frames the bill as adding remedies rather than creating the right from scratch.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers bear the cost of judgments, since the United States is made liable for officers' conduct with no exception when an officer would otherwise be immune from suit. Individual federal law enforcement and immigration officers face personal civil liability, including punitive damages up to $100,000 per violation, and their agencies bear the cost of annual training. More litigation against agencies is a foreseeable cost of the bill's design.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and federal law enforcement officers

drawbacks.text: Because the United States is liable regardless of whether the officer has any immunity defense, taxpayers would foot the bill for judgments even in cases where the officer would have won on qualified immunity, and critics would argue the $25,000 automatic damages invite a wave of litigation.

The bill covers only federal law enforcement and immigration officers, not the state and local police who carry out the vast majority of arrests and street-level enforcement, so it would leave most police encounters untouched.

The bill gives officers a defensible concern about on-the-job hesitation: the right is lost only if a person physically restricts or restrains an officer, so line officers would have to judge in the moment whether a bystander standing close to or in front of them is protected conduct, which the bill expressly says it is.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who witness or document federal policing, the bill would turn an uncertain constitutional argument into a concrete, fee-supported lawsuit with guaranteed minimum damages — a real remedy where today the usual path, a lawsuit under existing federal civil rights law, often fails against immunity defenses. The costs are real but limited: payouts come from the Treasury, the bill covers only federal officers, and its carve-out still lets officers act against anyone who physically interferes with an arrest. The main design criticism is that automatic $25,000 damages plus immunity waiver could generate suits that cost taxpayers more than the misconduct itself warranted; the main limitation is that it does nothing about state and local police.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action on it, so it has never come up for a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the Right to Record Act of 2026 on June 8, 2026; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
One Senate Democrat cosponsored the bill; no Republican has signed on.
The action history shows no committee hearings, no markup, no floor vote, and no further activity after the June 8 referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal law enforcement agencies, including immigration enforcement, are better off for now because no new liability, training mandate, or damages regime exists. People who film police continue to rely on case-by-case First Amendment litigation without the statutory damages or attorney's fees the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal law enforcement agencies, for now

for.name: Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill in the Senate.

for.name: 1 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it drew no other support.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on June 8, 2026 and has taken no action since — no hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred, but the sponsor and its only cosponsor are Democrats and no Republican has joined, in a Senate where Republicans hold 55 of 100 seats.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement agencies (including immigration enforcement)
industries.note: The bill makes the agencies financially liable for officers who interfere with recording, strips the shield of sovereign immunity for these claims, and requires annual training. Federal policing and immigration enforcement would face more lawsuits and payouts, which is the direct counterweight to the public's new remedy.

Judgments, statutory damages, and attorney's fees would be paid with public money, even where the individual officer would have had an immunity defense. This is the fiscal cost of a remedy designed to deter officer misconduct.

analysis.trajectory: With only a single cosponsor and a Republican-controlled Senate and Judiciary Committee, the bill is very unlikely to receive a hearing or a floor vote before the 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027; it will most likely die in committee and would need to be reintroduced, with substantially more support, to go anywhere.
